title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every interval per query versus an offline sweep with a min-heap keyed by size, lazily discarding expired intervals.

sections.title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query

content.title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an array of intervals [left, right] and an array of query points, for each query, find the size (right - left + 1) of the SMALLEST interval that contains that query point. If no interval contains a query, the answer for it is -1.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Smallest containing interval, for many query points\"","Process queries in sorted order, adding qualifying intervals to a pool as we go, using a min-heap keyed by size"],["Intervals can \"expire\" (their end passes the current query)","A min-heap allows removing expired intervals lazily as they surface at the top"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

For a query point q, only intervals whose left endpoint is at most q, and whose right endpoint is at least q, are candidates; among these, the smallest one (by size) is the answer. Processing queries in ascending order, and adding intervals to an active pool as their left endpoint becomes eligible, means the pool only ever grows in the "left-eligible" sense, and a min-heap by size can answer "which currently eligible interval is smallest" instantly, discarding any that have "expired" (right endpoint fallen below the current query).

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Smallest Available Parking Spot Near a Given Time
blocks.text: Picture parking spots each available during a specific time window, sized differently, and for various arrival times, wanting the smallest available spot that covers that arrival time. Processing arrival times in order, adding spots to an "available" pool as their start time passes, and removing spots whose end time has already passed, lets a size-ordered structure (like a min-heap) instantly answer each query.

blocks.caption: Sort queries ascending; sweep intervals into an active pool as their start qualifies; use a min-heap by size

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Result: [3, 3, 1, 4]. For query 4, interval [4,4] (size 1) is the smallest containing interval.
5. How Should We Think?

Before scanning all intervals for every single query, notice that sorting BOTH intervals (by left endpoint) and queries (ascending) lets a single sweep add each interval to an "eligible" pool exactly once (when its left endpoint qualifies), and a min-heap keyed by interval size lets each query be answered by peeking the smallest CURRENTLY VALID (not yet expired) interval.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An interval is a valid candidate for query q only if its left endpoint is <= q and its right endpoint is >= q.

Observation 2: Processing queries in ascending order means the "left endpoint <= q" condition only ever admits MORE intervals over time, never fewer, so intervals can be added to a pool incrementally via a pointer into the start-sorted interval list.

Observation 3: The "right endpoint >= q" condition means some previously-added intervals may become invalid (expired) as q increases; a min-heap keyed by size, when peeked, may need to discard expired intervals (those with right endpoint < current query) before finding a valid one.

Observation 4: Since each interval is added to the heap exactly once and removed (whether used or expired) at most once, the total heap operations across all queries are bounded, giving an efficient overall solution.

This leads to sorting both structures, sweeping intervals into a min-heap (keyed by size) as their left endpoint qualifies for the current query, discarding expired intervals from the heap's top, and reading the top (if any) as each query's answer.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each query, scan every interval directly, checking containment and tracking the smallest one found.
Step by step algorithm

items: For each query point q, scan every interval.
If the interval contains q (left <= q <= right), track its size, keeping the minimum found.
Record the minimum size found (or -1 if none contain q) as the answer for that query.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Scanning every interval per query directly implements the definition, correct regardless of order.
This costs O(intervals times queries), unnecessary once sorting both and sweeping with a min-heap avoids repeated scanning.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(intervals times queries).
Space: O(1) extra beyond the output.
Limitation: sorting both intervals and queries, then sweeping with a min-heap keyed by size, reduces the total time to O((intervals + queries) log intervals).
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why scanning every interval per query is wasteful: as queries are processed in increasing order, the set of "left-eligible" intervals only grows, so each interval only ever needs to be considered for ELIGIBILITY once.

The min-heap for size ordering: among all currently eligible intervals, a min-heap keyed by size lets the smallest one be found in O(log intervals), rather than scanning all of them again for every query.

Handling expiration: an interval's right endpoint might fall below the current query even though it was once eligible; these "expired" entries are discarded LAZILY, only when they surface at the top of the heap and are found to no longer be valid.

The core idea: sort both intervals and queries, sweep intervals into a min-heap as they become left-eligible, and lazily discard expired entries when answering each query.

Sort intervals by left endpoint; sort queries (keeping original indices) ascending. Sweep: for each query, add all newly-eligible intervals (left <= query) to a min-heap keyed by size; pop any expired intervals (right < query) from the heap's top; the top (if any) is the answer for that query.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for intervals = [[1,4],[2,4],[3,6],[4,4]], queries = [2, 3, 4, 5] (already sorted)

blocks.caption: Sweep intervals into a min-heap by size as they qualify; lazily discard expired ones at the top

codes.python:
import heapq

def min_interval(intervals, queries):
    intervals = sorted(intervals)
    sorted_q = sorted(range(len(queries)), key=lambda i: queries[i])
    result = [-1] * len(queries)
    heap = []                                             # (size, right endpoint)
    i = 0
    for qi in sorted_q:
        q = queries[qi]
        while i < len(intervals) and intervals[i][0] <= q:      # sweep in newly eligible intervals
            l, r = intervals[i]
            heapq.heappush(heap, (r - l + 1, r))
            i += 1
        while heap and heap[0][1] < q:                              # lazily discard expired intervals
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        if heap:
            result[qi] = heap[0][0]
    return result

blocks.text: Why This Works

Processing queries in ascending order means the pointer into the start-sorted intervals list only ever moves forward, adding each interval to the heap exactly once when it becomes left-eligible. The min-heap, keyed by size, always surfaces the smallest interval among those currently in it; discarding entries whose right endpoint has fallen below the current query correctly removes intervals that no longer contain it, since once expired, an interval can never become valid again for a LARGER future query. This guarantees the heap's top (after discarding expired entries) is always the correct, smallest, currently valid interval for each query.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((intervals + queries) log intervals), each interval pushed and popped from the heap at most once, plus the two sorts.
Space: O(intervals) for the heap.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Scan every interval per query","O(intervals times queries)","O(1) extra","Correct, but too slow for up to 10^5 of each."],["Sort both, sweep with a min-heap by size","O((intervals + queries) log intervals)","O(intervals)","The expected, efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Minimum Interval to Include Each Query is a strong example of the "offline sweep with a min-heap" technique, processing queries in sorted order while lazily managing an eligible-and-not-yet-expired pool of candidates.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to process queries in sorted order (via their original indices), losing track of which answer belongs to which original query position.

Discarding expired heap entries eagerly for every possible query rather than lazily only when they surface at the top, which would be less efficient but not incorrect; the key mistake is forgetting to discard them at all.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A query not contained in any interval","Correctly returns -1 for that query."],["Multiple intervals of the exact same smallest size containing a query","Any of them can be reported, since only the SIZE is asked for, not which specific interval."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "sort queries, sweep intervals in by start, min-heap by size, lazily discard expired" captures the full technique cleanly and shows command of the offline-sweep-with-heap pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "smallest/best candidate containing a point, across many query points", think: sort queries, sweep eligible candidates into a min/max-heap, lazily discard expired ones.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also report WHICH interval was the smallest, not just its size?
How would you handle intervals or queries arriving online, without knowing all queries upfront?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Meeting Rooms II, using a similar min-heap-based sweep technique for a different purpose (counting overlapping meetings).
Any "offline sweep with sorted queries and a heap for the currently valid candidates" problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Scanning every interval per query costs O(intervals times queries) time; the sort-and-sweep-with-heap approach costs O((intervals + queries) log intervals) time and O(intervals) space, the standard efficient solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: offline sweep, sorting queries ascending and sweeping eligible intervals into a min-heap keyed by size, lazily discarding expired entries.
Core Idea: as each query is processed, add newly left-eligible intervals to the heap, discard those whose right endpoint has expired, and read the heap's top as the answer.
Time: O(intervals times queries) for the brute force, O((intervals + queries) log intervals) for the optimized sweep.
Space: O(1) extra versus O(intervals) for the heap.
Most Important Observation: processing queries in sorted order lets each interval be added to the eligible pool exactly once, with a min-heap answering "smallest currently valid" instantly.
Interview Difficulty: a hard, well-known combination of sorting, sweeping, and heap-based lazy deletion.
One line memory trick: sort queries, sweep intervals into a min-heap by size, lazily pop expired ones.
